title: Class 5 Maths Word Problems with Solutions: A Step-by-Step Method + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 5 Maths Word Problems with Solutions
meta_desc: Solve class 5 maths word problems with a simple 4-step method and fully worked case studies across fractions, money and measurement, plus a free quiz.
excerpt: Most Class 5 children can add and multiply just fine — they get stuck deciding what to do. Here is the four-step method I use to crack mixed, multi-step word problems, with several worked solutions.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Class 5 child the sum 2,480 ÷ 8 and most will solve it without blinking. Wrap the same numbers in a story — ‘A shopkeeper packs 2,480 sweets equally into 8 boxes’ — and suddenly the pencil stops. This is the real hurdle. Class 5 maths word problems are rarely hard because of the arithmetic; they are hard because the child has to decide what to do before doing it. In my experience teaching ten-year-olds, that deciding step is exactly what we forget to teach.

The good news: there is a method, and it works across every Class 5 topic — large numbers, fractions, decimals, money and measurement. It is the same four steps every time, so a child stops guessing and starts thinking. NCERT calls this problem-solving; I just call it not panicking.

The four-step method for any word problem

Whether the problem is about rupees, litres or kilometres, the process does not change. Teach these four steps until they become automatic.

StepWhat the child doesThe question to ask
1. UnderstandRead twice; underline the numbers and the questionWhat am I being asked to find?
2. Plan the stepsDecide which operations, and in what orderIs this one step or two?
3. SolveDo the arithmetic carefully, one line at a timeAm I keeping my units straight?
4. CheckRe-read the question; does the answer make sense?Would this answer surprise a grown-up?

Notice that three of the four steps are not arithmetic at all. That is deliberate. A child who reads carefully and plans first makes fewer mistakes than one who dives at the numbers.

Why multi-step problems trip children up

Class 5 is the year word problems grow a second step. A Class 4 problem asks one thing; a Class 5 problem hides a smaller question inside a bigger one. Consider: ‘Riya buys 3 notebooks at ₹45 each and pays with a ₹200 note. How much change does she get?’ The child cannot answer the real question — the change — until they answer a hidden one first: the total cost. Miss that hidden step and the whole answer collapses.

So the single most useful habit I drill is the pause after reading: is this one step or two? If two, name the hidden question out loud before touching a number.

Worked case study 1: money and change

‘Riya buys 3 notebooks at ₹45 each and pays with a ₹200 note. How much change does she get?’

  • Understand: Find the change. We know price per notebook, quantity, and amount paid.
  • Plan: Two steps. First the total cost (multiply), then the change (subtract).
  • Solve: Total = 3 × ₹45 = ₹135. Change = ₹200 − ₹135 = ₹65.
  • Check: ₹135 spent plus ₹65 change is ₹200 — the note she paid with. It fits.

Worked case study 2: fractions of a quantity

‘A water tank holds 60 litres. Arjun uses three-fifths of it to water the plants. How many litres are left?’

  • Understand: Find the litres remaining, not the litres used.
  • Plan: Two steps. Find three-fifths of 60, then subtract from 60. (Or, cleverer: find the two-fifths that are left.)
  • Solve: One-fifth of 60 is 12, so three-fifths is 36 litres used. Left = 60 − 36 = 24 litres.
  • Check: Two-fifths of 60 is 2 × 12 = 24. Same answer by the shortcut. Confident now.

The classic trap here

Children read ‘three-fifths’ and hand back 36 as the answer, because that was the number they worked out. But the question asked what is left. This is why step 4 exists — re-reading the actual question catches the most common mark-losing error in the whole paper.

Worked case study 3: measurement with decimals

‘A ribbon is 2.5 metres long. A tailor cuts off 4 pieces of 0.4 m each. How much ribbon is left?’

  • Understand: Find the leftover length in metres.
  • Plan: Two steps — total cut (multiply), then subtract from 2.5.
  • Solve: Cut = 4 × 0.4 = 1.6 m. Left = 2.5 − 1.6 = 0.9 m.
  • Check: 1.6 m used plus 0.9 m left is 2.5 m. The decimals line up.

A few honest tips that actually help

Estimate before you solve. If a child guesses the change on Riya’s notebooks is ‘about ₹65’ before calculating, a slip that gives ₹650 gets caught instantly. Estimation is not extra work; it is a free safety net.

Watch the units. Half the measurement errors I see come from mixing metres with centimetres or rupees with paise in the same line. Convert everything to one unit first, then calculate.

And here is the counter-intuitive one: slow readers often score higher on word problems than fast calculators. The child who reads the story twice and plans beats the one who spots two numbers and multiplies them on reflex. Speed is not the goal in Class 5 — correct planning is.

quiz.title: Class 5 Maths Word Problems Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight mixed word problems covering money, fractions, decimals and measurement. Read each twice, decide if it is one step or two, then pick your answer.

questions.q: Riya buys 3 notebooks at ₹45 each and pays with a ₹200 note. How much change does she get?
questions.explanation: Total cost = 3 × 45 = 135. Change = 200 − 135 = 65. Two steps: multiply, then subtract.

questions.q: A tank holds 60 litres. Arjun uses three-fifths of it. How many litres are LEFT?
questions.explanation: One-fifth of 60 is 12, so three-fifths (used) is 36. Left = 60 − 36 = 24, which is the two-fifths remaining.

questions.q: A ribbon is 2.5 m long. A tailor cuts 4 pieces of 0.4 m each. How much is left?
A shopkeeper packs 2,480 sweets equally into 8 boxes. How many sweets per box?
A book has 240 pages. Meera reads one-fourth on Monday and 30 pages on Tuesday. How many pages has she read in all?
questions.explanation: One-fourth of 240 is 60. Then 60 + 30 = 90 pages. Two steps: fraction, then add.

questions.q: Pens cost ₹12 each. How many pens can you buy with ₹100?
questions.explanation: 100 ÷ 12 = 8 with 4 left over. You can buy 8 pens; you cannot buy a ninth.

questions.q: A jug holds 1.5 litres. Three glasses of 0.2 litres are poured out. How much juice remains?
A farmer harvests 5,600 kg of wheat and sells 3,750 kg. How many kilograms are left?
questions.explanation: 5,600 − 3,750 = 1,850 kg. A one-step subtraction with large numbers.

faq.q: Why does my child struggle with word problems but not plain sums?
faq.a: Because word problems test a different skill: deciding which operation to use, not just doing it. A child fluent in multiplication can still freeze when a story hides the multiplication inside two steps. Teaching the read-plan-solve-check method fixes the deciding part.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake in Class 5 word problems?
faq.a: Answering the wrong question. A child works out the part they were asked to find along the way — say, the amount used — and forgets the question asked for the amount left. Re-reading the actual question at the end catches this every time.

faq.q: How do I teach multi-step problems without confusing my child?
faq.a: Have them name the hidden first step out loud before writing anything. For a change-from-a-note problem, the hidden step is the total cost. Once they say ‘first I need the total’, the second step becomes obvious.

faq.q: Should my child estimate before solving?
faq.a: Yes, always. A quick estimate — ‘the answer should be about ₹65’ — acts as a safety net that catches decimal-point and place-value slips instantly. It takes seconds and saves marks.
